title: Speaking Part 3 — two jobs every turn
note:
Derived from dialogues-data.json. Nothing invented: the correct option is the real turn, and the two distractors are that same turn with one half removed.

The tags in the source are the design. Thirty-two labels, and almost all of them have the form <respond>_then_<advance>: partial_agreement_then_disagreement, acknowledging_then_building, agreeing_then_speculating. That is Part 3 in one line — every turn has to do two jobs, answer your partner and move the discussion on.

The failure it teaches against is two students taking turns to deliver prepared opinions at each other. Cambridge assesses Interactive Communication mainly in Part 3, and a turn that ignores the partner scores badly however good the English is.

So: distractor A is the turn with its responding half stripped (your point, but deaf). Distractor B is the responding half alone (polite, and the conversation stops).

bankNote:
Every phrase here is lifted from a turn in these eight discussions — nothing was written for the list.

What was LEFT OUT is the point. The Advanced register in the source produces 'Indubitably', 'I concur entirely', 'That constitutes a legitimate consideration' and 'That possesses practical value'. Indubitably appears five times. That is not C1, it is a thesaurus, and handing it to a fifteen-year-old to say aloud would do them harm in the room. Those phrases stay in the dialogues, where a student meets them in context; they do not go in a list headed 'phrases to use'.

Also left out: the sentence-splitter caught a few first turns whose opening sentence carries real content rather than a response — 'I honestly think schools should ban phones', 'Because people just message instead of meeting up'. Those are opinions, not acknowledgements, and they are not responding moves.
